summary: Applies the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). Checking a packet's TTL or hop limit shows whether it came from a node on a directly connected link, which protects a router's control plane from CPU-exhaustion attacks. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A guard checks that visitors really came from next door and not from far away. If a message looks like it traveled a long way, it gets turned away.

questions: how to secure ldp with gtsm
what is the generalized ttl security mechanism
what is the ldp g flag
subtitle: How LDP routers use a TTL check to refuse peering attempts from anyone who is not directly connected.

tldr.problem: LDP routers accept packets from remote senders, so forged protocol packets from outside the network can burn router CPU in an attack on the control plane.
tldr.mechanism: Each LDP router sets a new G flag in its Link Hello to say it supports GTSM. If both sides set it, each requires incoming LDP/TCP packets from that neighbor to carry a TTL or Hop Count of 255.
tldr.outcome: Off-link attacks against single-hop LDP sessions become much harder. The cost is that sessions which are really multi-hop, or set up with Extended Discovery, are not protected and can even fail to come up.

facts.label: New flag
facts.value: G, in the Common Hello Parameters TLV

today: RFC 6720 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5036, and the unit metadata shows it has itself been updated by RFC 7552. Read it together with that RFC.

sections.title: Why LDP Needs GTSM
sections.content:
LDP (RFC 5036) has two ways to find peers, both over UDP. Basic Discovery finds peers that are directly connected at the link level. Extended Discovery finds neighbors that are not directly connected. Once found, the two Label Switching Routers (LSRs) set up a peering session over TCP.

The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM, RFC 5082) checks the IPv4 Time To Live or IPv6 Hop Limit of incoming packets. It gives a simple and reasonably robust defense against infrastructure attacks that use forged protocol packets from outside the network. RFC 6720 says exactly how LDP uses it.

GTSM itself says it SHOULD NOT be enabled by default, to stay compatible with unmodified protocols. So this RFC adds a built-in negotiation: two peers use GTSM only if both detect that the other supports it and agree. The wish to use GTSM is on by default, with no configuration.
sections.eli5: Imagine only letting in visitors who say they live on your street. LDP routers use a quick check to make sure the other router really is a close neighbor.

sections.title: What Is and Is Not Covered
sections.content:
The RFC covers LDP over IPv4 routing. LDP over IPv6 is not covered because GTSM is built into the protocol definition there, according to a separate work-in-progress document.

It also covers only single-hop LDP sessions, in line with Section 5.5 of RFC 5082. Features that depend on multi-hop LDP sessions, such as LDP IGP Synchronization or LDP Session Protection, do not work with GTSM. They need the GTSM capability disabled, either statically or dynamically.
sections.eli5: The guard only works for next-door neighbors. If a friend lives several streets away and needs to visit, the guard has to be told to let them in.

sections.title: The G Flag in the Hello Message
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new flag in the Common Hello Parameters TLV of the LDP Link Hello message. It is the G flag (for GTSM), carried in a bit that RFC 5036 had reserved. That is why this RFC updates RFC 5036.

An LSR sets G=1 to say it supports GTSM procedures and G=0 to say it does not. The flag sits next to the existing T (Targeted Hello) and R (Request Send Targeted Hellos) flags. The remaining reserved bits MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The G flag only matters when T=0, which is always the case for Basic Discovery. Otherwise the receiver ignores it. An LSR that does not know about the G flag simply keeps ignoring it, as RFC 5036 already requires.
sections.eli5: The G flag is a small tick box on a hello card. Ticked means "I will do the neighbor check", and unticked means "I will not".

sections.title: Sending Hellos and Starting the Session
sections.content:
Basic Discovery Hellos go to the link-level multicast address 224.0.0.2 ("all routers"). They are never forwarded beyond one hop, and are RECOMMENDED to carry an IP TTL or Hop Count of 1. Unless configured otherwise, an LSR that supports GTSM MUST set G=1 in these Hellos.

What happens next depends on what the neighbor said:

  • If the LSR sent G=1 and received G=1, it MUST enforce GTSM on the TCP connection with that neighbor. That means checking that incoming unicast packets for the LDP/TCP session have a TTL or Hop Count of 255, then handling them as RFC 5082 says.
  • If the neighbor sent G=0, or does not recognize the flag, the LSR MUST NOT enforce GTSM for that session.

The second rule keeps older routers working and switches GTSM off automatically when the two sides do not agree.
sections.eli5: Two neighbors each say "I will check where visitors come from." Only if both say yes do they start checking. If one says no, they skip the check so they can still be friends.

sections.title: Peering Scenarios and Exceptions
sections.content:
GTSM negotiation is on by default for Basic Discovery but not for Extended Discovery, because Basic Discovery usually means a single-hop session and Extended Discovery usually means a multi-hop one. The RFC lists three exceptions:

  • Two adjacent LSRs (for example back-to-back PE routers) form a single-hop session after Extended Discovery. GTSM is not enabled by default.
  • Two adjacent LSRs form a multi-hop session after Basic Discovery, because of how IP routing is set up. GTSM is enabled and enforced, so the session is prevented from forming. This can hurt features such as LDP IGP Synchronization and LDP Session Protection.
  • Two adjacent LSRs do both discoveries. GTSM is enforced for the Basic one only. If both use the same IPv4 transport address in both, there is a single session and it has GTSM. Otherwise the Extended session does not.

To handle all of these, implementations may offer a way to enable or disable GTSM per peer, by configuration or dynamically.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a close neighbor looks far away, or a far-away friend looks close. The rules allow the guard to be switched on or off for each visitor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it makes LDP more resilient to off-link attacks. The security considerations of GTSM itself are in Section 5 of RFC 5082.

Two limits are called out. First, a single-hop session set up with Extended Discovery may not get GTSM, so LDP can still be exposed to forged packets. Second, GTSM can stop a session from forming, or tear it down, if routing ever says the directly connected peer is more than one IP hop away. For those cases the RFC recommends cryptographic integrity, such as the TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925), especially for multi-hop sessions.

RFC 5082 says the messages used to negotiate GTSM MUST be authenticated, but LDP discovery runs over UDP and has no authentication. GTSM is also not a substitute for authentication and does not stop insider on-the-wire attacks. The multicast address used by Basic Discovery is never forwarded beyond the link, which gives basic protection against off-the-wire attacks.
sections.eli5: The neighbor check keeps out strangers from far away, but it cannot stop someone already inside the street. For stronger protection you also need a secret password.
